planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, alkaline clay soil in late summer so crimson stigmas can be hand-picked at dawn in autumn.

directions: Corms are planted in the clay-rich plains around San Gavino Monreale in Sardinia's Campidano, a landrace strain protected under Italy's DOP saffron designation. Flowers emerge in October and the three crimson stigmas must be plucked by hand each morning before the bloom wilts, then gently dried to concentrate their aroma. The resulting saffron threads flavor Sardinian dishes such as fregula and malloreddus alla campidanese. Plant in full sun with sharp drainage, since standing winter moisture rots the corms.

planting.note: Plant rooted dormant cuttings in spring on well-drained limestone slopes and train as a low, unirrigated bush vine to concentrate sugars.

directions: Xynisteri is Cyprus's principal indigenous white grape, cultivated for centuries on the dry limestone and chalk slopes of the island's high-altitude villages. It is the backbone of the fortified sweet Commandaria wine when sun-dried and blended with the red Mavro grape, and is also vinified fresh into crisp, low-acid dry whites. Vines are traditionally dry-farmed and trained low to the ground as bush vines to withstand drought and summer heat. Harvest typically occurs in late August to early September once sugars peak.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring in dry, rocky soils and prune to a low bush form; the vine tolerates drought but ripens slowly, so avoid overly fertile sites.

directions: Mavro is Cyprus's traditional dark-skinned grape, one of the two ancient native varieties alongside Xynisteri that together form the base of Commandaria, among the oldest named wines still produced today. Its thick skin and moderate sugar levels make it well suited to the long sun-drying process used before fermentation of that dessert wine, though it is also pressed into light, pale red table wines locally. Bush-trained vines are dry-farmed on hillside terraces across the Commandaria villages south of the Troodos mountains, with harvest usually following Xynisteri by a few weeks in early-to-mid autumn.

planting.note: Set out grafted trees after all frost danger has passed, in full sun with sharp drainage; fruit colors and sweetens fully only after cool winter nights.

directions: This historic orange originated on Malta and was exported to France in the 18th and 19th centuries, where it became known as the 'Maltaise' and gave its name to the classic hollandaise variation, sauce maltaise, made from its intensely perfumed, lightly blushed juice. The flesh carries only a faint rosy mottling compared to deeply pigmented Sicilian blood oranges like Moro, but its floral aroma is distinctive. Trees need a frost-free site with well-drained soil and benefit from winter chill to develop the blush and sugar-acid balance. Fruit ripens through the winter months and is typically picked from December into February.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered, wind-protected spot in full sun after frost danger passes; this citrus is cold-sensitive and needs a mild coastal Mediterranean microclimate.

directions: Pompia is an unusual, deeply dimpled citrus found almost nowhere outside the Baronia district around Siniscola in northeastern Sardinia, and is widely believed to be an ancient spontaneous hybrid between citron and bitter orange or lemon. The huge, bumpy-skinned fruit has a thick, intensely fragrant peel but very bitter, sparse juice, so the pulp is rarely eaten fresh. Instead the peel is parboiled to reduce bitterness, then candied and layered with honey and toasted almonds to make the traditional Sardinian sweets aranzada and mandorlata di pompia, especially around Christmas and Carnival. A Slow Food Presidium now supports the handful of growers still tending these heirloom trees.
